objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how your eyes work in the dark, read airport and airplane lights, list the night equipment rules, and spot and manage the extra risks of flying at night.
why: The airplane flies the same at night, but the pilot does not: you see less, judge distance worse, and are easier to fool [[24:218|AFH 11-1]]. Knowing your limits and the lights turns night flying from scary to routine.

prereading.what: The whole night operations chapter: vision, illusions, equipment, lighting, preflight, takeoff, landing, emergencies.

prereading.what: Vision in flight, night blind spot, dark adaptation, scanning, night vision protection, night illusions.

warmup: You finish a sunset flight with a friend. Sunset was 30 minutes ago. Is it 'night' yet? Does the answer change depending on whether you are asking about lights, logging, or carrying your friend?

key_terms.def: End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight, converted to local time.
The time when the sun's center is between the horizon and 6 degrees below it.
Eye cells mostly around the edges of the retina that see in dim light, in shades of gray, with little detail. They make night vision possible.
Eye cells packed in the center of the eye that see color and detail in good light. They do not work well at night.
The center 5 to 10 degrees of your view, where there are no rods. Dim things you look straight at can disappear.
Your eyes slowly getting more sensitive in the dark. Full adaptation can take up to 30 minutes.
Looking about 10 degrees to the side of an object so the rods can see it.
Airport lights you turn on by clicking your mike on a set frequency.
A still light seems to move when you stare at it in the dark.
Approach over dark water or land where only the runway lights show. It makes you feel high, so you fly too low.

body.p: The rules use three different 'nights'. Learn which one goes with which rule.

head: Rule
Time period
What it controls
rows: End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight [[60:11|14 CFR 1.1]]
Logging night time, night equipment (91.205(c)), night fuel and weather minimums
Position lights must be on (anticollision lights, if installed, stay on day and night)
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]

body.p: Civil twilight is the time the sun's center is between the horizon and 6 degrees below it. Evening civil twilight starts at sunset and ends when the sun's center is 6 degrees below the horizon [[24:218|AFH 11-1]].

Night currency: to act as PIC carrying persons from 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise, you need 3 takeoffs and 3 landings to a full stop in the last 90 days, made in that same time window [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]. You must have been the sole manipulator of the controls, in the same category, class and type (if a class or type rating is required) [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].

callout.text: Lights: sunset to sunrise. Log it: civil twilight. Passengers: 1 hour after sunset, 3 full-stop landings in 90 days.
Night landings for currency must be to a full stop. Touch-and-goes do not count [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].

check.q: Your last night full-stop landings were 100 days ago. Can you take a friend flying at 9 p.m., two hours after sunset?
check.a: No. You need 3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings, 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise, within the preceding 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]. Fly 3 night full-stop landings without passengers first.

chunks.title: How your eyes work in the dark

body.p: Your retina has two kinds of light cells [[24:218|AFH 11-1]]:

bullets: Cones sit mostly in the center (the fovea is all cones). They see color and fine detail in good light [[24:218|AFH 11-1]].
Rods sit mostly around the edges. They see in dim light, in shades of gray, with no detail and no color [[24:218|AFH 11-1]].
At night, seeing depends almost entirely on the rods [[24:219|AFH 11-2]].

head: Type of vision
When
What happens
rows: Cones work. Sharp detail and color [[24:219|AFH 11-2]]
Cones and rods both work. Detail and color fade [[24:220|AFH 11-3]]. PHAK calls this the most dangerous time for seeing [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]]
Only rods really work. Acuity drops to 20/200 or less [[1:443|PHAK 17-21]]

body.p: The night blind spot: the fovea has no rods, so the center 5 to 10 degrees of your view goes blind in low light [[24:220|AFH 11-3]]. If you look straight at a dim object, it may not show up, or it may fade away after you see it [[24:220|AFH 11-3]].
You also lose depth perception and size judgment at night, not just color and sharpness [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].

callout.text: To see something dim, don't look right at it. Look slightly to one side.

check.q: Why can a dim airplane disappear when you stare straight at it at night?
check.a: The center of your eye (fovea) has no rods. In the dark that center 5 to 10 degrees is a night blind spot [[24:220|AFH 11-3]].

body.p: Dark adaptation: your eyes get more sensitive the longer you are in the dark. Full adaptation can take up to 30 minutes [[24:220|AFH 11-3]]. The AIM adds that you can get a moderate amount in 20 minutes under dim red cockpit light [[34:186|AIM 8-1-6]].

bullets: Looking at a bright light (landing lights, searchlights) for 1 second or more ruins it for a while [[24:220|AFH 11-3]].
Anti-collision flashes are shorter than 1 second, so they do not hurt your adaptation [[24:220|AFH 11-3]].
If bright light comes, close one eye to save that eye's night vision [[24:220|AFH 11-3]].

body.p: Scanning at night: look left to right (or right to left), starting far away and moving in. Scan about 30 degrees per stop, no more than 2 to 3 seconds each stop, and overlap the last area by 10 degrees [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].
Off-center viewing: look about 10 degrees above, below or beside the object [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]]. Don't hold one spot longer than 2 to 3 seconds or the image fades [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].
Things that hurt night vision:

head: Factor
Effect
rows: Night vision declines measurably above 4,000 ft pressure altitude [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]. AFH warns of hypoxia above 5,000 ft at night [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]
Smokers lose 20% of night vision at sea level, like being at 5,000 ft [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]]
Bright sun earlier in the day
Slows dark adaptation. Wear N-15 (neutral density) sunglasses in daytime before a night flight [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]
Pilots stare and stop scanning; vision and judgment suffer [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]]
Lack of it impairs night vision [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]]

body.p: Cockpit light: keep it as low as possible [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]. Red light keeps night vision but distorts chart colors (magenta and yellow look red) [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]. Use dim white light to read charts [[24:221|AFH 11-4]].

check.q: You flip on the bright white dome light for 5 seconds to find a pen. What happened to your dark adaptation, and how could you have saved some of it?
check.a: 1 second or more of bright light impairs night vision [[24:220|AFH 11-3]]. Closing one eye saves that eye's adaptation [[24:220|AFH 11-3]]. A dim red or dim white flashlight is better.

body.p: Rotating beacons help you find the airport. They flash 24 to 30 times per minute for airports [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9]].

head: Beacon colors
Means
rows: White, white, green (two quick white flashes)

callout.text: A beacon on in daytime often means weather below 3 miles and/or 1,000 ft in Class B, C, D or E surface areas, but don't rely on it. There is no rule that says it must be on [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9]].

head: Light
Color
rows: White. On instrument runways, yellow on the last 2,000 ft or half the runway, whichever is less (caution zone) [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]]
Red toward the runway (end), green toward landing airplanes (threshold) [[33:126|AIM 2-1-4]]
Yellow (flashing elevated pair or in-pavement row) at runway holding positions [[33:133|AIM 2-1-10]]
Red across the taxiway. Never cross a lit red stop bar, even if cleared [[33:134|AIM 2-1-10]]

body.p: Obstructions: flashing red beacons (20 to 40 flashes per minute) and steady red lights at night [[33:135|AIM 2-2-3]]. High-intensity flashing white lights mark tall towers and wire-crossing structures [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].
Pilot-controlled lighting (PCL): key the mike on the listed frequency [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

bullets: Lights stay on 15 minutes from the last time you clicked [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].
Always click 7 first, then lower if you want [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].
Click again when you get close or just before final, even if the lights are on, to get a full 15 minutes [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].
The frequency is in the Chart Supplement, not on the sectional [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

check.q: You click 7 times on the CTAF 10 miles out and the runway lights come on. Why click again on downwind?
check.a: Receivers may need you close to work, and the lights stay on only 15 minutes from the last activation. Clicking again close in makes sure you get the full 15 minutes [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

chunks.title: Airplane lights and reading other traffic

body.p: For VFR at night, 91.205(c) adds these to the day VFR list [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]]:

bullets: Approved position lights.
An approved aviation red or white anticollision light system.
One electric landing light, if operated for hire.
An adequate source of electrical energy for all installed electrical and radio equipment.
One spare set of fuses, or three spare fuses of each kind required, accessible in flight.

callout.text: FLAPS: Fuses, Landing light (for hire), Anticollision lights, Position lights, Source of electricity.

body.p: From sunset to sunrise, position lights must be on [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)]]. Parked or moving in or near a night flight operations area, the airplane must be clearly lit, have its position lights on, or be in an area marked by obstruction lights [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(a)(2)]]. If you have anticollision lights, they must be on any time you operate, day or night, but the PIC may turn them off when that is safer (for example, glare in clouds) [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209(b)]] [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].
Position lights work like a ship's: red on the left wingtip, green on the right wingtip, white on the tail [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

head: You see
The other airplane is
rows: Red on the left, green on the right
Flying the same direction as you. Keep clear [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]
Green on the left, red on the right
Coming toward you. Could be a collision course [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]

callout.text: Red-right? Watch out, you're in its sight (head-on). Red-left is like your own airplane: same direction.

body.p: Other airplanes' lights can blend with stars and city lights. Make a real effort to pick them out [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]. Scanning at night depends almost entirely on peripheral vision [[16:13|AC 90-48E para 13]].
Help others see you: the FAA encourages landing lights on below 10,000 ft, day or night, especially within 10 miles of any airport [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]].

check.q: Ahead and at your altitude you see a green light on the left and a red light on the right. What does that mean?
check.a: The airplane is coming toward you; it could be a collision course [[24:223|AFH 11-6]]. Turn away and keep it in sight.

chunks.title: Night navigation, charts and your flight bag

body.p: Personal equipment to have within reach [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]:

bullets: At least one reliable flashlight, ideally dimmable with white and red light, plus spare batteries [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].
White light for the preflight walkaround, red for the cockpit, dim white for charts [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].
Aeronautical charts, including the adjacent chart if your route is near the edge [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].
Flight data and a checklist (before start, before takeoff, cruise, before landing, after landing, stopping engines, emergencies) [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].
An EFB is fine, but turn its brightness down [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].

body.p: Organize the cockpit and place charts and gear within easy reach before you taxi [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].
Chart reading at night:

bullets: Draw course lines in black so they show in low light [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
Good night checkpoints: airport beacons, lighted obstructions, city lights, and highway traffic [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
On the sectional, 'L' means runway lights on dusk to dawn. '*L' means limits apply, so check the Chart Supplement (part-time, on request, or pilot-controlled) [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]].
A star by the airport means a rotating beacon operates dusk to dawn [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]].
Red light makes magenta and yellow chart symbols look red; use dim white light for charts [[24:221|AFH 11-4]].

body.p: GPS: load all waypoints before flight and check the database before takeoff and again in flight [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]. Monitor position, time, and fuel just as in the day [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

City lights can be seen at surprising distances. Without the adjacent chart you may not know what you are looking at [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]. At 2,000 ft a group of lights may look separate; at 5,000 ft or higher they may blend into one mass [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

callout.text: Before a night cross-country, check the destination's lighting in the Chart Supplement and NOTAMs [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

check.q: Your sectional shows '*L' by an airport. What should you do before planning to land there at night?
check.a: Check the Chart Supplement. '*L' means lighting limits exist, such as part-time, on request, or pilot-controlled lighting [[2:15|Chart Users' Guide p. 15]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: a night flight

body.p: This Task has only Knowledge and Risk Management elements, so there are no ACS flight tolerances to meet. The examiner will test it by questions and may combine it with other tasks flown at night. The AFH procedure:

bullets: 1. Preflight: check weather with extra care for temperature/dew point spread (fog) and wind [[24:224|AFH 11-7]]. Turn on every airplane light briefly; tap position light fixtures to find loose connections [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]. Walk the ramp with a flashlight for chocks, ladders and holes [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

2. Start: organize the cockpit. Clear the propeller area with extra care. Beacon on or flash the position lights to warn people. Leave extra electrical gear off until the engine is running [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]. Position lights on before start at night [[24:53|AFH 2-16]].
3. Taxi: taxi or landing light on, but watch electrical load and overheating. Don't blind other pilots. Taxi slowly and follow the taxi lines. Check instruments while taxiing [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
4. Stay sure of where you are: the taxi diagram, signs, markings and instruments should all agree. If anything is in doubt, stop. Don't continue the taxi or takeoff [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
5. Run-up: hold or lock the brakes and watch for creeping forward. You can't easily see it at night [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

6. Takeoff: dim cockpit lights to the lowest usable level. Landing and taxi lights on, line up on centerline, check heading. Keep between and parallel to the edge lights. Check instruments often [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].
7. Climb: confirm a positive climb on attitude indicator, VSI and altimeter, at best climb speed [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]. No turns until a safe maneuvering altitude [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

8. Arrival: fly toward the beacon until you can see the runway lights. Identify the threshold and edge lights and keep them in sight [[24:227|AFH 11-10]]. Do the before-landing checklist early; set the heading bug to the runway [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].

9. Approach: fly normal speeds and a normal glidepath. A low, shallow approach is wrong at night. Cross-check altimeter and VSI, and use a VASI if there is one [[24:227|AFH 11-10]]. Landing light on about halfway down final [[24:227|AFH 11-10]].

10. Landing: hold the descent until the landing light shows tire marks on the runway, then round out smoothly [[24:228|AFH 11-11]]. With no landing light, start the round out when the far runway lights seem to rise above the nose [[24:228|AFH 11-11]].

body.p: Exterior lights on the ground [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]:

head: Situation
Lights
rows: Taxi light on; off when stopped or yielding [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]
All exterior lights on, at the PIC's discretion [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]
Entering runway for takeoff or line up and wait
Landing lights on when cleared, or starting the roll at a non-towered field [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]

callout.text: Runway incursion risk goes up in low visibility. Do heads-down tasks only while stopped. If you are unsure where you are, stop (not on a runway) and ask ATC for progressive taxi [[7:9|AC 91-73B]].
In line up and wait at night, consider lining up about 3 feet left or right of centerline so a landing pilot can tell you from the runway lights [[7:10|AC 91-73B]].

check.q: During a night run-up, why should you hold or lock the brakes and keep looking outside?
check.a: At night the airplane can creep forward without you noticing [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

body.p: Darkness makes it easier for your eyes to fool you [[24:221|AFH 11-4]].

head: Illusion
What happens
Fix
rows: A still light seems to move after you stare at it; movement starts in about 8 to 10 seconds [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]
Keep scanning. Don't stare at a light more than 10 seconds [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]
Stars and ground lights blend; a row of lights or a sloping cloud looks like the horizon [[24:221|AFH 11-4]]
Over water or dark land you feel higher than you are, so you fly too low and may land short [[24:222|AFH 11-5]] [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]
Use VASI/PAPI or glideslope, flight instruments; go around if in doubt [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
Roads or trains look like runway lights. Bright runway lights make you feel closer, so you fly a high approach [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
Know the airport layout; check the altimeter
Few lights on the way in
The runway seems farther away, so you fly too low [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]
An airplane seems to move away when it is really coming closer [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]
You lock onto one thing (instruments or the runway) and miss everything else [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]

body.p: Runway shape and slope also fool you, day and night: a narrow or upsloping runway makes you feel high (you fly low); a wide or downsloping runway makes you feel low (you fly high) [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
How to prevent landing errors [[24:230|AFH 11-13]]:

bullets: Expect illusions at unfamiliar airports, especially at night.
Check airport diagrams and the Chart Supplement for runway slope, terrain and lighting.
Look at the altimeter often on every approach.
Use VASI/PAPI or an electronic glideslope when available.
Know that distractions and emergencies raise approach accident risk.
Stay proficient at landings.

check.q: You are landing at night on a runway on a dark shoreline with no lights around it. Which way will the illusion push you, and what do you use to stop it?
check.a: Black-hole/featureless terrain makes you feel high, so you tend to fly too low and may land short [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Use a VASI/PAPI or glideslope and your instruments, and go around if in doubt [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].

chunks.title: Night risks: currency, weather and broken equipment

body.p: Currency is not proficiency. 61.57(b) is a minimum. Most pilots fly only a small part of their time at night, and marginal weather at night is a big deal, so judge your own need for more practice [[15:20|AC 61-98E para 3.1.2]].
The AFH says even experienced pilots should fly night VFR only with unrestricted visibility, favorable winds on the surface and aloft, and no turbulence [[24:231|AFH 11-14]].
Weather you can't see:

bullets: Clouds are hard to see at night. The first sign of flying into one is ground lights slowly disappearing [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].
A halo or glow around ground lights means ground fog. Be careful continuing that way [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].
A small temperature/dew point spread may mean fog [[24:224|AFH 11-7]]. Clear, calm nights favor radiation fog [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]].
Wind is harder to judge at night, so pay attention to forecast wind [[24:224|AFH 11-7]].

head: Night rule
Requirement
rows: Enough to reach the first point of intended landing plus 45 minutes at normal cruising speed (day is 30 minutes) [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)]]
Class G, 1,200 ft AGL or less

3 SM visibility; 500 below, 1,000 above, 2,000 horizontal from clouds [[60:465|14 CFR 91.155]]. Exception: 1 SM and clear of clouds in the traffic pattern within 1/2 mile of the runway [[60:466|14 CFR 91.155(b)(2)]]
Class G, above 1,200 ft AGL, below 10,000 MSL

body.p: Inoperative equipment:

bullets: Required night items (position lights, anticollision lights, electrical source, fuses) can't be deferred for a night flight [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]] [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].
Without an MEL, other broken items may be deferred only if not required, deactivated or removed, placarded INOPERATIVE, and judged not a hazard [[60:493|14 CFR 91.213(d)]].
If an anticollision light fails in flight, you may continue to a stop where it can be repaired [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)(3)]].

PHAK's example: position lights found inoperative can be deferred for a daytime flight (switch off, placarded INOPERATIVE) [[1:240|PHAK 9-10]]. Not for a night flight, because 91.205(c) requires them.

body.p: Distraction and disorientation: a small problem, like an instrument light failure, can grab your attention and push out more important tasks [[24:51|AFH 2-14]]. Over water at night the horizon can blend with the water, and stars can reflect on it [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]. Don't fly into dusk or darkness unless you are proficient with flight instruments [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

callout.text: If you meet IMC at night, risk goes up dramatically unless the pilot and airplane are IFR-ready with an IFR plan you can activate [[24:226|AFH 11-9]].

check.q: You find the left position light burned out during preflight at dusk. Can you go?
check.a: Not at night. Position lights are required for night VFR [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]] and must be lit sunset to sunrise [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]]. Get it fixed first.

body.p: Night mistakes the AFH and PHAK warn about:

head: Error
Why it happens / fix
rows: No visual references ahead, so new pilots relax right rudder [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]
No turns until a safe maneuvering altitude [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]
Distance and height are hard to judge. Use altimeter, VSI and VASI [[24:227|AFH 11-10]]
Few visual cues. Wait for the landing light to show tire marks [[24:228|AFH 11-11]]
Ruins outside vision and makes reflections. Dim to the minimum [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]
Landing light in haze or cloud
Reflection and distortion. Turn it off once the climb is established, unless used for traffic [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]
Causes autokinesis and the night blind spot. Keep scanning [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]
Locked on instruments or the runway, missing traffic and ground closure [[1:449|PHAK 17-27]]
Missing the airplane creeping during run-up
Hold or lock the brakes and look outside [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]

callout.text: If you are ever unsure of your position or altitude relative to the runway on a night approach, go around [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].

check.q: On your first night takeoff you drift left right after liftoff. Why?
check.a: With few visual references ahead, inexperienced pilots tend to relax right rudder after takeoff and veer left [[24:225|AFH 11-8]].

scenario.title: Taking a friend home after dark
scenario.setup: You are a new private pilot. Your last night landings were 4 months ago. A friend wants a ride to a small airport 60 miles away; you would leave 90 minutes after sunset. The destination has a 3,000-ft runway with pilot-controlled lighting next to a dark lake, no VASI. The forecast is clear and calm, with temperature 12°C and dew point 10°C. During preflight you notice the right position light flickers when you tap it.

questions.q: Can you legally carry your friend tonight?
questions.a: No. You need 3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings between 1 hour after sunset and 1 hour before sunrise within the past 90 days [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]]. Four months is too long. Even after getting current, AC 61-98E says to judge your need for more proficiency, not just currency [[15:20|AC 61-98E para 3.1.2]].

questions.q: What does the weather tell you?
questions.a: A 2°C spread on a clear, calm night points to possible fog [[24:224|AFH 11-7]] [[1:299|PHAK 12-15]]. Watch for halos around ground lights or lights fading out, the first signs of fog or cloud [[24:226|AFH 11-9]]. Plan an alternate, and carry at least the night VFR minimum: fuel to the destination plus 45 minutes at normal cruise [[60:464|14 CFR 91.151(a)(2)]].

questions.q: What about the flickering position light?
questions.a: The AFH says if a light blinks when tapped, find the cause before flight [[24:225|AFH 11-8]]. Position lights are required for night VFR [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]], so have it fixed before going.

questions.q: What illusion should you expect at the destination, and how will you handle it?
questions.a: A runway by a dark lake with no surrounding lights sets up a black-hole approach: you feel high and fly too low [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]. With no VASI, use the altimeter and a normal pattern, and go around if unsure [[24:222|AFH 11-5]]. Click the mike 7 times to get full lights, and again close in [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

questions.q: How do you protect against collisions and runway incursions on the ground there?
questions.a: Taxi slowly with lights as the AIM suggests, keep the taxi diagram out, and stop if anything doesn't match [[24:225|AFH 11-8]] [[33:266|AIM 4-3-24]]. At a non-towered field, scan the full runway and final before entering [[7:7|AC 91-73B]].

questions.q: Your friend starts chatting during the approach. What do you do?
questions.a: Distractions raise approach accident risk [[24:230|AFH 11-13]]. Brief a sterile flight deck before the flight (no talking during departure and arrival) [[1:64|PHAK 2-25]], and politely ask for quiet on approach.

quiz.q: To carry passengers at night, your 3 takeoffs and 3 full-stop landings must be within the preceding 90 days and made during what period?
options: End of evening civil twilight to beginning of morning civil twilight
1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise
30 minutes after sunset to 30 minutes before sunrise
quiz.why: 61.57(b) uses 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise [[60:238|14 CFR 61.57(b)]].

quiz.q: Position lights must be on during which period?
options: 1 hour after sunset to 1 hour before sunrise
Only in Class B, C or D airspace at night
End of civil twilight to beginning of civil twilight
quiz.why: 91.209 requires lighted position lights from sunset to sunrise [[60:491|14 CFR 91.209]].

quiz.q: Why should you look about 10 degrees to the side of a dim object at night?
options: To reduce glare from cockpit lights
Because the center of the eye has no rods and is blind in low light
Because cones are more sensitive off center
quiz.why: The fovea has no rods, so the center 5 to 10 degrees is a night blind spot [[24:220|AFH 11-3]]. Off-center viewing uses the rods [[1:445|PHAK 17-23]].

quiz.q: At night you see another airplane with its green light on your left and red light on your right. It is:
options: Flying the same direction as you
Crossing from right to left and moving away
Heading toward you, possibly a collision course
quiz.why: Red on the right and green on the left means it is coming toward you [[24:223|AFH 11-6]].

quiz.q: With pilot-controlled lighting, keying the mike 7 times within 5 seconds:
quiz.why: 7 clicks gives the highest intensity available [[33:132|AIM 2-1-8]].

quiz.q: Which item is NOT required by 91.205(c) for a private, not-for-hire night VFR flight?
quiz.why: A landing light is required only if the aircraft is operated for hire [[60:487|14 CFR 91.205(c)]].

quiz.q: A black-hole approach over dark water usually makes a pilot:
options: Feel too low and fly a high approach
Feel too high and fly a low approach
See the runway as wider than it is
quiz.why: Featureless terrain makes you feel higher than you are, so you fly too low and may land short [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[24:222|AFH 11-5]].

quiz.q: A rotating beacon flashing white and green identifies:
quiz.why: White and green means a lighted land airport [[33:133|AIM 2-1-9]].

takeaways: Three nights: lights sunset to sunrise; logging and equipment at civil twilight; passenger currency 1 hour after sunset, 3 full-stop landings in 90 days.
Rods see at night; don't stare. Scan in short stops and look 10 degrees off center.
Protect dark adaptation: dim cockpit lights, avoid bright light, no smoking, oxygen and rest help.
Red-right means head-on traffic. Know beacon, runway (white/red/green) and taxiway (blue/green) colors, and click 7 for PCL.
Expect illusions on approach. Use VASI/PAPI and the altimeter, and go around if in doubt.
Currency is a minimum. Fly night VFR only in good weather, with all required lights working.
cfi_notes: Have students explain the three different 'night' periods; mixing them up is the most common oral-exam error.
Demonstrate dark adaptation on the ramp: brief students to avoid the FBO's bright lights before boarding.
Do the PHAK blind-spot test (PHAK 17-21) and the moon test in class (PHAK 17-22) so students feel the night blind spot.
On the first night flight, show the 'lights disappear' sign of a cloud layer and how hard it is to see clouds.
AFH recommends practicing maneuvers with cockpit lights off as well as on, and blackout landings as an emergency procedure (AFH 11-7, 11-11). Unusual attitudes at night only with an instructor.

Sources differ slightly: AFH 11-7 says yellow runway edge lights cover 2,000 ft from the far end; the AIM limits this to instrument runways, last 2,000 ft or half the runway. The lesson teaches the AIM.
Flicker vertigo frequency differs between sources (AFH 11-4: 1 to 20 Hz; PHAK 17-27: 4 to 20 cycles per second). Not quizzed.
Examiners often ask: night equipment (FLAPS), PCL clicks, beacon colors, position light interpretation, night currency, and how to handle an electrical failure at night.
Alaska applicants: the ACS note points to 14 CFR 61.110 for night flying exceptions.
gaps: Airplane-specific night items (landing/taxi light duty limits, electrical load, interior lighting controls, night checklist items) must come from the POH/AFM.
The sources do not give position light coverage angles or detailed rules for anticollision light colors beyond 91.205(c)(3).
Night-specific electrical failure procedures depend on the POH; the AFH covers night engine failure (AFH 11-13) but not a full electrical failure checklist.
14 CFR 61.110 (Alaska night exception) was not reviewed in this lesson.
